- If sentiment is strongly bullish (≥ 0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly to avoid overshoot.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤ 0.33) or neutral (0.00), model often underestimates; adjust upward to reflect mean reversion or hidden support.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overcorrects and forecasts a prolonged upward trend — cap forecast growth to avoid lagged overreaction.
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish (or vice versa) within 3–5 days, model fails to adjust quickly; apply a “sentiment lag” correction: reduce forecast by 1–2% per day of sentiment divergence.
- Model consistently underestimates true outcomes in the first 5–7 days of a new trend — apply a “trend lag” bias: add 2–5% to forecast for early days if sentiment is bullish.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 70) after a spike, model often fails to recognize — reduce forecast by 1–3% per day of reversion.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to ignore sentiment volatility — if sentiment swings >0.33 in 3 consecutive days, apply a “sentiment volatility penalty” to forecast: subtract 0.5–1.5% per swing.
